analytic.title: Simultaneous Multi-Objective Optimisation for Low-Power Real-Time Networks-On-Chip

div.p: Simultaneous configuration of task mapping and network routing is a way to address the schedulability issues in the Networks-On-Chip embedded hard real-time systems. The approach provides alternative routes as a way to reduce interferences from high-priority messages, but without a guarantee that the network routes produced are low in power dissipation. This drawback is due to the lack of insight on the power dissipated by the Networks-On-Chip. We propose a multiobjective optimisation technique with a macromodel to minimise power dissipation while maintaining the schedulability of the systems. The results from the experimental work show that the proposed technique could find a good trade-off between the two objectives.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In a Networks-On-Chip (NoC), a task mapping allocates tasks to processing cores while a network routing protocol routes messages on network links. The utilisation of the system resources (cores and links) is scheduled based on the priority pre-emptive scheduling policy [1]. In a worst-case scenario, however, a contention between tasks or messages to get access on the NoC resources may cause deadline misses (Fig. 1a). One way to relieve a contention is by changing the task mapping and network routing in the NoC as shown in the example of Fig. 1b. With the new task mapping, tasks are allocated to cores in a way that the routing protocol could provide better network routes. The new network routes reduce the contention between messages, but as depicted in Fig. 1b the network route between T 2 and T 6 is longer than the previous route (Fig. 1a). As a result, the increased number of links causes the power dissipation to increase. Table I displays the impact of the increased number of links on power dissipation. On the other hand, the route between task T 1 and task T 5 is shorter than the previous route in Fig. 1a. Indeed, this shows a potential that the amount of power dissipation could be reduced, given that the optimisation algorithm aware of the power dissipated by NoC. Otherwise, the reassigning of network links will only be feasible to relieve contention, but will not be able to minimise power dissipation. In this paper, we address the above problem by proposing a new approach with the aim to find a configuration that is schedulable and dissipate low power. This is achieved by introducing a multi-objective optimisation with two fitness functions based on the schedulability analysis and link power dissipation, integrated with simultaneous exploration of task mapping and network routing. The proposed approach addresses the problem by finding the best trade-off between the two objectives.

The rest of the sections is structured as follows. Section II explains the background of this work and section III describes the application and hardware models used for the proposed approach. In section IV, we describe the proposed approach in detail, including the fitness functions and the optimisation process. Section V reports the results from the experimental work and lastly we conclude this work in section VI.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: A researcher [2] proposed an algorithm to meet the hard real-time requirements, but the task mapping is constructively produced, hence it is not optimised and may prohibit alternative tasks mappings from being found in the design space.

Task mapping optimisation approaches such as [3], [4] apply Genetic Algorithm (GA) and the schedulability analysis [5] to find task mappings for NoC. As shown in their results, a schedulable NoC is achievable by merely optimising the task mapping. However, in some cases where network links are shared by many messages, congestion could easily occur and without alternative routings the approaches could render the system unschedulable.

In a network with deterministic routing, a packet is routed on network links between the sender and receiver according to a pre-determined network route. An example of this type of routing is XY routing and such routing scheme is realised in the implementation of Hermes [6], QNoC [7] and Dally [8]. Some state-of-the-art optimisation techniques [9], [10] involving configuration of multiple parameters assume that the NoC routing protocol is deterministic in their system models. This hinder their approaches from finding schedulable routes.

Multiple parameters optimisation is one way to meet design requirements, but the exploration of those parameters may increase the optimisation time. A technique to configure task mapping and network routing was proposed by [11] for multimedia application. The configuration is performed in stages; task mapping and then followed by network routing. It addresses the problem, but the duration to explore the design space could increase. Other approaches such as [12], [13] repeats the routing and evaluation for swaps between nodes. Repetition in the configuration and evaluation could impose a significant delay to the optimisation time.

Power and speed may conflict each other. For example, more power is required by systems with fast performance as compared to systems with slow performance. Mapping communicating tasks closer to each other may reduce a NoC's power dissipation due to the reduced number of routers and links to deliver messages. As a consequence, tasks are accumulated in the same area, increasing the contention which could affect the end-to-end response times.

For a hard real-time system, it is essential that the end-toend response time of each task must not exceed the deadline. Otherwise the system will become unschedulable. Multiobjective energy-aware NoC task mapping approaches [14]- [16] only address problems in average cases. The energy dissipation is calculated depending on how much hops packets take to arrive at destinations for the best-effort systems. However, it lacks the analysis for verifying schedulability. Based on the XY routing in [17] a mapping algorithm was proposed to minimise energy and meet the bandwidth constraints. The algorithm [17] was further extended [18] to optimise routing. However, again it does not support schedulability analysis for hard real-time embedded NoC. Again, all the approaches [11]- [13] do not support the hard real-time requirements. A technique proposed by [19] apply the schedulability analysis for optimising task mapping and routing at the same time. However, such technique lacks insight on NoC power dissipation. How much power dissipated from NoC, however schedulable it is, was unknown.

To the best of our knowledge, the simultaneous exploration of task mapping and the message routing with schedulability and power dissipation optimised for NoC-based hard real-time embedded systems is still an open problem. Techniques that can address this problem are essential to find feasible configurations with a good trade-off between power and schedulability within a reasonable optimisation time.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL A. Application
div.p: Application model is used to describe the characteristics of computation and communication load imposed by an application. In our model, task and message releases are either sporadically or periodically. A transmission of message is after the originating task completes its execution and no overhead from the NoC's Network Interface (NI) are taken into consideration. Hence, in a worst-case scenario the upper bound of the task's end-to-end response time is defined as the time since release until the last packet arrives at the destination.

Every task is described as a tuple T = {c, t, p, d}, where c is the task's worst-case execution time, t is its minimum inter-arrival interval, p and d is the task's priority level and the end-to-end deadline respectively. The worst-case execution time (WCET) of a task is defined as the maximum time to finish execution when no other tasks runs at the same time over a processing core.

A message is packetised into several packets before transmission. The packets are sent over the NoC's links from a source to a destination in series. Each message is described as a tuple F = {So, De, P, L, C}, where So and De is the transmitting task and the receiving task respectively, P is the priority level of the message, L is the message's length and the message's maximum basic latency is C. The C is the latency when no other messages run with the message over a network path. Given a specific path on the NoC and the maximum packet size of a message is known, it is calculated based on the total hops on the path, the total flits, the total time a flit required to traverse a link and the total time a router needed to route and arbitrate packet headers.

div.head: B. System Platform
div.p: The platform model consists of a system with an on-chip multicore and a NoC interconnection. We implemented the hardware platform as a 2D Mesh with wormhole switching and deterministic routing scheme. The arbitration unit is based on flit-level pre-emption, using priority levels to regulate access of tasks and messages on shared cores and links respectively. More than one task can run on a processing core and a link can support multiple messages.

div.head: IV. MULTI-OBJECTIVE OPTIMISATION A. Power Macromodel
div.p: The power dissipation macromodel is based on the estimation in [20]. It is used to calculate the total power dissipated by a NoC to transfer a packet. Every network component such as network interface NI, router and link dissipates power to transmit a packet along the specified route. Our equation (1) calculates the dissipation of power by each NoC's component as follows:
where f and h is the number of flits in the packet and the number of hops of its route respectively.

For a flit transmission, P ni is the power dissipated by the NI, P r is the power dissipated by the router and P l is the power dissipated by the link. In our macromodel, it is assumed that the amount of power dissipated by a router to transmit a payload flit or a header flit is equal.

div.head: B. Schedulability Analysis
div.p: The fitness function to verify schedulability is based on the end-to-end schedulability analysis [10]. It is formulated to determine the schedulability of each task and message in the system. In order to reduce the complexity of the analysis, it is assumed in the system model that a task's deadline is equivalent to its period or d = t. At the same time, the deadline of message follows the same deadline of its originating task. For each task i, given the worst-case response time r i and the deadline d i of task T i , then the task is deemed schedulable if r i ≤ d i . Otherwise, if task T i is unschedulable, the value of U T i becomes one. A value zero indicates that the task is deemed fully schedulable.
div.formula: T i : if r i > d i ⇒ U T i = 1
div.p: The message F i 's release from a source task T i is after the latter completes its processing. Since the overhead to packetise payload is negligible, the maximum release jitter for the message can be deduced as (r i ) of the task. Subsequently, the end-to-end response time can be calculated as the time from the task is released until the last packet arrives at the destination. If the the end-to-end response time fail to meet the T i 's deadline, then the message may not be schedulable. For example, this could occur due to the interference from other packets sharing the same path or to the delay of the task execution itself. Only if r i + R i ≤ d i , where R i is the worst-case latency of message F i , a message is deemed as schedulable. Otherwise, the value of attribute U F i becomes one. A value zero indicates that the message is deemed fully schedulable.
div.formula: F i : if r i + R i > d i ⇒ U F i = 1
div.p: The amount of unschedulable tasks and messages, as calculated by equation ( 2), is the metric that represents the schedulability of the system. In other word, the system is deemed as fully schedulable if the metric is zero or S = 0.
div.formula: S = k i=1 U T i + l i=1 U F i(2)

div.head: C. Design Space
div.p: The proposed GA-based algorithm manipulates the threadlike structure known as chromosome to encode information on the configuration. Every chromosome is a possible configuration of mapping and routing for the system. The chromosome in Fig. 2 is divided into small units called genes and are grouped to present mapping and routing respectively. The first half with the green genes contains information on the task mapping. Each gene represents a task and contains an index of a processing core as its mapping location. A processing core is allowed to accommodate more than one tasks. Therefore, the same index can appear multiple times in more than one genes. For example, the 1st gene (task τ 1 ) and the 3rd gene (task τ 3 ) contains index five, hence the tasks are mapped on the same processing core. The other half of genes marked by orange colour contains the network routing information. Every orange gene represents a message in which contains network packets. The NoC's network routing protocol determines a network route for the message between the source and destination. Then, the message will travel through several nodes on its network route. A node on the route can be altered to divert the message from receiving interferences. As a result, another route is produced in addition to the previous one created by the network routing protocol. Based on this notion, each orange gene is programmed to contain the index of a router. For example, the first orange gene from the left represents message 1 . It shows an index 3. First, the message must travel through the router, before continuing to the destination. The role of the network routing protocol is to determine the new route for this message.

div.head: D. Optimisation Objectives
div.p: Our approach is based on GA. The algorithm follows the evolutionary principles in such a way that a population is continuously evolved to produce better individuals over a number of generations. The evolution involves several processes that manipulate the chromosomes of individuals. These processes, as shown in Fig. 3, are selection, crossover and mutation. The selection process is responsible for finding the best parents for the crossover process based on a binary tournament. The parents' chromosomes are then combined by the crossover process to produce more than one offspring. The offspring becomes the new individuals in the population. Some of the parents are transferred to the population without being mated and this probability is determined by the crossover rate. A diversity is introduced into the population by mutating some of the genes in the individuals. The probability of a gene to be selected for mutation are determined by the mutation rate. The first objective (Obj 1 ) function, as shown in equation ( 3), is the minimisation of total power dissipated by the NoC for transmitting packets. To compute the power dissipation metric the objective function uses equation ( 1). The energy dissipated by the execution of tasks by each individual core is excluded from our optimisation process because that metric does not facilitate the ranking of mappings in the population. This is based on the assumption that all cores are homogeneous and will dissipate nearly the same amount of energy to execute a particular task.
div.formula: Obj 1 = min( l m=1 P m )(3)
div.p: The second objective (Obj 2 ) function ( 4) is the minimisation of the total number of unschedulable tasks and messages. Equation ( 2) is used to compute the metric S.
V. EXPERIMENTAL WORK

div.head: A. Evaluation Setting
div.p: The evaluation was conducted based on two types of test bench: realistic and synthetic, to gain a thorough understanding on the performance of the proposed approach. The former was derived from an application in an autonomous vehicle, consisting 33 tasks and 38 messages. Meanwhile, the latter was synthetically created with 50 tasks and 50 traffic messages to represent more communication-intensive application. Both test benches follow the application model explained in subsection III-A. The test benches are labelled as Autonomous Vehicle Application (AVA) and Synthetic Application (SA) respectively.

The goal of the experimental work is to evaluate the proposed approach, afterwards known as GA-M algorithm, not only in terms of schedulability but also power dissipation. This experimental work is based on a hypothesis that the proposed technique is able to find a schedulable configuration (task mapping and network routing) with a good trade-off in power dissipation. For this purpose, a baseline known as GA-S algorithm was constructed based on the same optimisation setting as shown in Table II. Population represents the number of configurations in a population at every generation. The value of generations is the number of iterations performed by the algorithms. Crossover and mutation rates are attribute values for the evolution process. Both algorithms have a similarity in terms of optimisation flow as depicted in Fig. 3. The only difference is the way optimisation was performed, GA-S runs a single-objective optimisation while GA-M runs a multi-objective optimisation. For GA-S, power dissipation was calculated based on the same macromodel in sub-section IV-A after the optimisation was completed. Although, this might seems GA-M had an advantage, the multi-objective optimisation must consider finding the best trade-off between two criteria. According to the concept of Pareto efficiency, it is impossible for GA-M to change a configuration to gain the best result in one criterion, without affecting the rest of criteria. In other word, there is no guarantee that the power dissipation would be the lowest in the population with 100% schedulability.

The sizes of NoC platform on which the test benches were mapped is variable in size. Two sizes of 2D Mesh NoC architecture namely 4x4 and 5x5 are known to produce good results [20] with GA. Thus, the same platform sizes were selected as a benchmark to study GA-M.

div.head: B. Evaluation Results
div.p: A comparison with GA-S infers that GA-M performs better in terms of power dissipation. Fig. 4 and 5 depict these performance as the optimisation progressed through generations. From Fig. 4a power dissipation yielded by GA-M is lower than GA-S. At the start of optimisation between 0 to 13 generations, both algorithms show slight differences. As the generations increased, GA-M's power dissipation gradually decreased lower than GA-S. Both algorithms successfully met the schedulability objective (zero unschedulable tasks and messages), but GA-M's schedulability convergence is faster than GA-S. As shown in Fig. 4b, GA-M converged at 13 th generation as compared to GA-S at 45 th generation.

Similar to the AVA on a 4x4 platform, GA-M recorded better power dissipation in comparison with GA-S for SA on a 5x5 platform. Fig. 5a depicts the comparison of power dissipation between both algorithms. At the 40 th generation, the levels of power dissipation are not much different. The improvement on the power dissipation becomes apparent as the optimisation proceeded above 40 th generation. For the schedulability, late convergence was recorded for GA-M at 144 th generation, later than 102 nd generation as recorded by The two objectives, power dissipation and schedulability, are both affected by the changes on task mapping and network routing. There are many ways to create a new route for relieving contention. A longer route maybe schedulable, but it could lead to an increased power dissipation. A good strategy is to find a good trade-off between both objectives. The main question is how good a trade-off can be improved by optimisation. Fig. 6 shows the improvement of configurations from the 1 st generation towards the 500 th generation where the GA-M achieved the Pareto efficiency. Both the Pareto efficiency curves are similar for both test benches (AVA and SA), but the power dissipation of the schedulable configuration is higher than the configuration at the low end of the curve. Nevertheless, this is the best trade-off achieved by GA-M with the selected number of generations.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: The proposed multi-objective optimisation provides a good trade-off between power dissipation and schedulability. Power dissipation becomes a concern if long routes are produced as the result of changing network routes. This issue is fully addressed by utilising the power dissipation macromodel and the schedulability analysis in our optimisation approach. Experimental results based on the realistic and synthetic test benches show that the configuration found by the proposed algorithm is better than the single-objective optimisation. In future work, we will extend our approach to support other parameters such as network buffer.
